For urban other roads on weekends, we recommend using hour ID 3 for hour IDs 1 and 2, as well as applying the speed distribution from hour ID 22 to hour IDs 23 and 24. With these small adjustments for late-night driving on other roads, all road and day types in MOVES could be updated with these speed distributions from FleetDNA. 30 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Figure 18. Speed bin distributions for FleetDNA combination-unit long-haul vehicles by hour Figure 19 displays the speed bin distributions for combination-unit short-haul trucks from FleetDNA. In comparison to Figure 18, the first thing we note is the lower data quality in terms of number of vehicles and recorded time for some categories (indicated by the pale shaded background). We also see that rural roads and urban freeways on weekends have distributions more concentrated on specific speeds due to this low data density, such as the top left graph, which has nearly 100% of recorded hours in the speed bin centered around 70 mph because very little driving time was logged during these hours. Most urban roads have better data quality and less sporadic hourly lines. While trucks driving at all hours on urban freeways on weekdays spend most of their time in speed bins between 60 and 75 mph, we see that the lines for hours near midnight (designated by purple and yellow colors) have higher proportions of time spent in the 70-mph bins and less time between 0 and 50 mph than the midday hours (green lines). For urban other roads, trucks spend time at speeds between 0 and 60 mph, with small peaks at 5 and 55 mph in a somewhat bimodal distribution. 31 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Figure 19. Speed bin distributions for FleetDNA combination-unit short-haul vehicles by hour Figure 20 displays speed bin results for single-unit short-haul trucks based on available logged data, which included only urban roads. In general, we again see freeways with a peak around 60 mph for various hours and other roads with a lower-speed peak. In this case, the low-speed peak for other roads is broad, with proportionally more of these trucks’ time spent between 0–35 mph and less spent at faster speeds for most hours compared to the combination-unit short-haul truck urban other category as seen in Figure 19.
